title: Why agentic AI will grow customer service demand, not shrink it
summary: Discover why agentic AI in customer service increases demand, transforms CX, and enables scalable, AI-powered engagement.
body_text: Why agentic AI will grow customer service demand, not shrink it by Andy Traba July 22, 2026 Share Nearly every AI business case for customer service begins with the same assumption: customer demand is finite. Take today’s interaction volume. Automate a percentage of it. Reduce the cost per interaction. Convert the difference into projected savings. The logic is sound. The assumption deserves another look — and the timing could not be more relevant. A Gartner survey of customer service and support leaders found 85% planned to explore or pilot customer-facing conversational generative AI. That unprecedented scale of experimentation means most enterprises are about to test, in real time, their demand assumptions. But what if today's interaction volume equals the amount of friction customers have been willing to tolerate and is not about demand at all? It’s common for customers to do a quick cost-benefit analysis before reaching out to a company. They ask themselves whether the issue is worth enduring hold purgatory? Or searching through a website, navigating a menu, verifying an account, explaining the situation – only to have to repeat every detail a second, third or fourth time? Something our friend Kristen Bell knew all too well before experiencing the NiCE effect . Sometimes it’s enough to make people want to avoid that scenario altogether. A customer ignores a minor billing question. A new user gives up on a feature they need help using. A buyer abandons a product comparison. An account owner postpones a configuration change. A traveler accepts an inconvenient option because resolving it would require too much time. These moments rarely appear in contact center data because they never become interactions. Yet they represent real customer needs, lost opportunities and, in some cases, early indicators of churn. AI changes the cost of serving that demand. It also changes the cost of expressing it. When assistance becomes immediate, conversational, contextual and capable of completing an action, customers may find more reasons to engage. What if making customer service dramatically faster, easier, and less expensive causes customers to use far more of it? Jevons Paradox When technology sharply reduces the effective cost of using a resource, demand often expands enough that total consumption of that resource increases rather than declines. Jevons Paradox: Why cheaper AI conversations increase demand Customer service can take a cue from British economist William Stanley Jevons' observation, giving CX leaders a lens to consider how behavior changes when the price of an activity falls. In 1865, Jevons examined Britain's industrial growth and dependence on coal. At the time, improvements in steam-engine efficiency were expected to conserve fuel. More efficient engines required less coal to produce the same amount of work. Jevons observed a broader effect: as steam power became more economical, businesses found more uses for it. Adoption expanded across factories, transportation and industry, contributing to greater overall coal consumption. The idea later became known as Jevons Paradox. When technology sharply reduces the effective cost of using a resource, demand often expands enough that total consumption of that resource increases rather than declines. We’ve seen efficiency expanding consumption many times. Lower-cost computing increased the number of calculations businesses could perform. A less expensive digital storage solution meant companies could retain far more data. Lower distribution costs helped transform software from a product purchased periodically into a service used continuously. Each efficiency gain changed the economics of supply. More significantly, each one expanded the range of economically viable uses. AI is having that effect on customer conversations right now. What is the abundance economy in customer service? For as long as contact centers have existed, demand has been rationed by two constraints: human capacity and cost. AI removes both at once, making an entire tier of conversations — too small or inconvenient to justify a human interaction — economically viable for the first time. That shift turns a scarcity economy into an abundance economy : high-quality customer engagement becomes less expensive and available enough to support far more of it than legacy staffing models allowed. As the marginal cost of a customer interaction decreases so does the threshold for starting one. We’re at the point now where the same customer issue that made a 15-minute call seem daunting may easily justify a 15-second exchange with an AI agent today. Traditional metrics may miss this hidden demand, because they only measure what customers already tolerated. Abundant service capacity reaches those moments earlier. This shows that real demand has become visible and affordable to serve. As cost approaches zero, that's an ideal outcome, but it also presents new potential challenges. Coordinating millions of customer conversations Scarcity economies are easy to manage because they're small: a modest set of agents, scripts, and systems can keep pace with a few thousand conversations a day. Abundance breaks that arithmetic. Millions of additional viable conversations mean the enterprise is coordinating an expanding web among customers, AI agents, employees, applications and enterprise systems, all needing the same accurate outcome. That complexity doesn't grow at the same rate as the conversations themselves: each new participant multiplies the relationships that must stay consistent, rather than adding to a list. That's the paradox at the center of the abundance economy where the same efficiency that makes more conversations possible also makes each one harder to get right, since there are more places for context to be lost and more moments where an answer without orchestrating intelligence can go off the rails. Why standalone chatbots and point AI solutions fail without scale The first wave of customer service AI focused on substitution with chatbots answering questions, copilots summarizing calls, classifiers routing intent — each solving a narrow problem well. Point AI is built to answer a question rather than coordinate an enterprise. That distinction becomes decisive as conversations become abundant. A standalone chatbot can resolve one request in isolation but typically can't see what a customer discussed with an agent last week or where a related workflow stands. Stack several such tools, each governed by different rules, and the result is AI that's individually competent but collectively incoherent. Gartner's 2025 research on customer service AI investment captures this shift directly: the most valuable AI use cases are no longer standalone chatbots but AI embedded across the full service operating model. That's because, in an abundance economy, the scarce resource is the context that makes it useful: a customer's history, the policy that applies, their verified identity, what they're permitted to do, where a workflow stands, what the product can and can't do, and what the organization already knows from prior interactions scattered across CRMs, knowledge bases, billing systems and employees' memories rather than any single point solution. Without a shared layer to assemble that context on demand, abundance produces millions of disconnected conversations instead of millions of successful outcomes. That's when a platform stops being a preference and becomes a necessity. 4 payoffs from shared intelligence on a CX AI platform If context is the scarce resource, the organizations that win will treat customer intelligence as shared infrastructure, not a feature bolted onto each channel — an operating system that every conversation draws from and writes back to, so the next interaction is as informed as the first. McKinsey's 2025 Global Survey on AI shows why most enterprises aren't there yet: 88% report regular AI use in at least one function and 62% are experimenting with AI agents, yet only 23% are actually scaling an agentic system anywhere. High performers, McKinsey finds, are nearly three times more likely to have fundamentally redesigned workflows around AI rather than layering it on top. This is the role of a CX AI platform , a connective layer of intelligence, orchestration and governance that lets every AI agent, employee and system operate from the same context, policy and source of truth. NiCE’s CX AI centers on exactly this — linking intelligence, orchestration and human expertise so AI moves beyond isolated automation toward complete, coordinated outcomes, growing more valuable as volume grows. At Fabletics, agentic AI authenticates the customer and completes a refund by coordinating the full path to resolution, bringing in humans when discretion or empathy is required. The value isn't a marginally cheaper refund — it's a policy-driven request resolved end to end, at a cost that makes handling it economically viable in the first place. Tripadvisor took its voice agent, Vesper, from concept to live calls in two and a half months — proof this shift can happen quickly. Built on NiCE AI Agents powered by Cognigy, Vesper captures intent, verifies identity, pulls information from multiple systems in parallel, and hands off full context the moment a human is needed. Early results show a 90% customer sentiment score on the interaction types measured, against 71% for the same interactions handled by people. Every handoff also strips a 2-minute identity-and-intent sequence out of the employee's workload. Toyota's E-Care shows what proactive engagement looks like at scale: more than 25 AI agents across voice and chat, watching for the moment a vehicle flags an engine warning, then contacting the owner, scheduling service, alerting the dealership and briefing the service team before the car arrives. Under the old model, that interaction often never happened — the warning was ignored, the call put off, the appointment never got booked. Now, 95% of customers who get the outreach book directly with the AI agent, and 98% respond positively. This is an interaction that wouldn't have existed otherwise, with safety, operational and revenue value attached. As these leading brands highlight, a CX AI platform pays off in at least four ways: Substitution with AI handling existing work more efficiently. Stimulated demand with customers asking questions they would have skipped. Proactive engagement with AI initiating contact before a customer has to. Expanded purpose with service as an entry point into adoption, retention and revenue work. A CX AI platform also compounds as an intelligence system. What’s fragmented across transcripts and tickets becomes visible across channels so teams see friction as it happens, not after renewal. But the platform still assumes conversations begin and end inside the enterprise's own channels. The next wave of interaction growth challenges that assumption. Agent-to-agent AI: How personal and enterprise agents will negotiate directly Interaction growth will likely accelerate further as customers delegate work to personal AI Agents — systems that monitor subscriptions, travel, or accounts and can initiate a conversation with an enterprise's AI agent directly. A task too small may still be worth pursuing automatically at machine speed. That shift is the inevitable consequence of everything before it: conversations that cost less enable more interactions at a scale outside what the old contact center was built to absorb. Consider what becomes routine once personal and enterprise AI agents are common. An airline’s operations agent contacts a hotel’s booking agent to extend a stranded traveler’s reservation after cancellation. A bank’s fraud agent coordinates with a customer's insurance claims agent to open a related claim without the customer repeating the story twice. A connected vehicle’s onboard agent negotiates a service appointment directly with a dealership’s scheduling agent. A procurement agent renegotiates supplier terms with a supplier’s own commercial agent ahead of renewal, escalating to a human only if the two can't converge. None of this is futuristic at this moment. What's new is that both sides of an exchange may be AI agents, acting for a human and an enterprise, without either watching in real time. What AI agent governance requires in identity, consent, and auditability When one AI agent acts for a customer and another for an enterprise, the question is no longer just “was the answer correct?” It becomes who authorized this exchange, whose identity is represented, what was the agent permitted to agree to, and does a human need to approve it before it's final? Without guardrails, this is a new category of risk since most enterprise AI programs have so far kept a human on at least one side of every exchange. Authorization and identity must work in both directions. Consent must be scoped and revocable, authorizing an agent to reschedule a flight not renegotiate a mortgage. Policy must be enforced inside the exchange itself since no human reviews every handshake, and auditability must be built in so decisions can be reconstructed later. Human oversight must be engineered on a unified foundation. This gap shows up in the data: Adobe's 2026 AI and Digital Trends report finds 63% of organizations expect agentic AI to free employees for more strategic work, but just 39% have a shared customer data platform capable of supporting it, and nearly one-third report misalignment between executives and the practitioners who must govern these systems. How an agentic engagement plane offers a trusted coordination layer Agentic AI native at the core of a platform changes the equation. Enterprises can now run AI agents, human teams, workflows, data, and systems as one intelligent operating model. NiCE’s Agentic Engagement Plane is built for a world where the parties to an interaction are a shifting mix of personal and enterprise AI agents, human experts and business systems. Where the CX AI platform assembles the context an enterprise needs to serve a customer, the agentic plane is the layer that governs how that context — and the authority to act on it — is shared with outside agents, enforcing exactly those safeguards in real time rather than after the fact. That coordinating plane is what Opus Research calls “the clipboard for the age of AI magic” in its Why Customer Experience Needs an AI Agent Control Plane report. That has to work across organizational boundaries that have never integrated before. The standards are still being written, but the direction is visible enough to build toward now. In a world with more AI agents, the plane will become a basic requirement so abundant engagement stays trustworthy and coordinated as the operating layer behind customer outcomes, as invisible to customers as payment networks are to commerce today. Will AI always increase customer service demand? When we talk about what Jevons Paradox means in relation to AI in customer service, we should be clear the economic theory doesn't guarantee AI increases demand everywhere. Better products may resolve issues before they need support, and some customers will prefer self-service with no conversation at all. Quality also determines the outcome: an inaccurate or intrusive AI experience suppresses demand by eroding trust, and disconnected, ungoverned interactions create outright risk. It depends on accurate knowledge, effective orchestration, human involvement and strong governance. As McKinsey's survey shows, most organizations still have work to do to scale AI enterprise-wide. Leaders should prepare for growing demand rather than assume volume stays fixed. AI will make customer service efficient and save costs. CX abundance will make service bigger. Orchestration will make service cohesive. Outcomes will make it more valuable. How CX abundance defines the next era of customer service Efficiency and cost-per-resolution metrics still matter, but they capture just part of the picture. A complete business case also asks how much additional demand becomes viable when service is immediate and scalable, and how much of it becomes coordinated outcomes rather than disconnected noise. That means tracking experience (is service trustworthy?), outcomes (adoption, retention, recovery?), prevention (what was avoided?), intelligence (what conversations taught the business), and, increasingly, coordination — whether agents, employees and systems share one governed view of the truth. For decades, interaction volume was treated as a measure of demand. It may be better understood as a measure of how much friction customers were willing to endure. The next era of customer service will be defined not just by how many needs an enterprise can resolve, but by how well it can coordinate an abundance of them into outcomes customers can trust. AI will make customer service efficient and save costs. CX abundance will make service bigger. Orchestration will make service cohesive. Outcomes will make it more valuable. Three questions can help leaders act on that shift now: Where is customer context still fragmented across disconnected tools? Which AI investments are optimized for containment rather than outcomes? And is the organization ready to govern AI agents that act on a customer's behalf, and go beyond just answering their questions? Enterprises that start answering those questions now can start building the CX AI coordination layer that customer service abundance requires instead of spending time managing the disconnected conversations. title: OT-IT convergence brings opportunities and risk
summary: Operational technology (OT) or industrial control systems (ICS) are responsible for keeping the power on and water and gas flowing to support essential services for consumers, industry and governments. As technology advances, utilities are introducing Internet connections (IT) to their OT networks to improve operational efficiency. They are also linking their OT systems to their IT systems to leverage the rich data being collected.
body_text: Operational technology (OT) or industrial control systems (ICS) are responsible for keeping the power on and water and gas flowing to support essential services for consumers, industry and governments. As technology advances, utilities are introducing Internet connections (IT) to their OT networks to improve operational efficiency. They are also linking their OT systems to their IT systems to leverage the rich data being collected. This OT-IT convergence is proving to boost performance and streamline ways of working by enabling capabilities such as off-site monitoring and remote maintenance. However, when it comes to cybersecurity, the majority of OT systems were developed in the 80’s and 90’s with little idea they would be part of a connected society, and thus with little thought to security. Because a cyber threat to IT is now becoming a cyber threat to OT as well, and vice versa, there’s no question that utilities must look at cybersecurity holistically across the two domains. But there are huge differences in how they operate―from cultures, to chains of command, to drivers, focus areas and job descriptions. In the OT environment, the focus is on high availability, and safety is paramount. Here, the impact of a cyber breach can include outages, physical injury and even loss of life. In the IT environment, which often supports back-office functions, operations are more controlled and managed. The impact of an IT breach tends to be financial or reputation loss, which can be very significant. A recent study by CGI in the UK, The Cyber-Value Connection has found that a severe cybersecurity breach represents a permanent cost of 1.8% of company value, as measured relative to a control group of peer companies. It may be logical to assume that an OT breach causing a widespread service outage and/or physical harm could have an even greater impact on valuation. The differences in OT and IT must be recognized to develop sound cybersecurity strategies in a connected world. Attempting to migrate security processes and tools from one side to the other is not a viable approach. But how can utilities (or other ICS industries like oil and gas or transportation) bring both sides together to ensure a common path to cyber vigilance? The high level of preparedness required to mitigate both OT and IT threats requires a holistic approach across the dimensions of people, process, technology and governance. Given the vast differences between OT and IT, utilities may need the expertise of strategic partners who understand both domains to help bridge the divide. The goal is an end-to-end cyber program that starts from the most basic levels (plant floor and field device) and moves up the organization through to the board room. (Read more on improving cyber governance in my colleague Andrew Rogoyski’s blog .) The following are recommended steps for developing a cybersecurity approach to support OT-IT convergence to achieve greater situational awareness and enterprise-wise visibility into threats and preparedness. Developing Cybersecurity GOVERNANCE PEOPLE PROCESS TECHNOLOGY Get the right people involved Determine what is OT and what is IT Develop a culture of vigilance Improve education Recognize the differences between OT and IT security Eliminate points of vulnerability Prepare for the worst case Create redundancy Establish priorities Monitor and test While OT and IT may be drastically different technology environments, the utilities industry is looking to combine these worlds, which means that vulnerability for attacks is higher, and protection is a first and foremost priority. CGI works with utilities and other ICS industries to understand and assess the criticality of their OT-IT security environments, identify gaps, determine where best to make investments, and assist with planning, implementation and operations. Learn more about this topic in our white paper, Convergence Brings Opportunities and Risk .

title: What makes a great product detail page? Defining the new standards for e‑commerce PDPs
summary: Learn what makes a product detail page that converts, from product images and mobile design to structured data and AI-ready catalogs.
body_text: In e‑commerce, products often have only seconds to make an impression. The brands that sell at first sight are increasingly the ones with the strongest product detail pages. In previous decades, only the biggest retailers could create high-performing product experiences. Smaller brands without access to photographers, post-production studios, or dedicated content and merchandising teams often struggled to compete. Today, that gap is narrowing rapidly. After analyzing tens of thousands of product detail pages across marketplaces, retailers, and direct-to-consumer brands, one pattern that we’ve observed at Photoroom is clear: the product pages that convert best are rarely defined by a single great image or clever piece of copy. They succeed because every element works together to remove friction and move customers toward a confident purchase decision. Shopping has always been visual, and product imagery remains one of the most important tools shoppers use to evaluate products online. As e‑commerce becomes more immersive, mobile-first, and visually sophisticated, the PDP has evolved from a source of product information into a critical conversion engine. Table of contents: What is a product detail page? Why the PDP has become the new storefront Defining the new standard for high-performing product pages Six essential jobs every product detail page should do The anatomy of great product page design Which e‑commerce brands are raising the standard Common PDP mistakes hurting conversion Future-proofing your PDPs for AI shopping agents Building scalable PDP systems across your catalog What is a product detail page? A product detail page (PDP) is the page that provides all the information shoppers need to evaluate and purchase a specific product online. It is the stage of the shopping journey where customers move from discovery to evaluation. A PDP typically includes product images, descriptions, variants, pricing, reviews, shipping information, and other supporting content. While every e‑commerce store is different, the purpose of a PDP remains the same: to help shoppers understand a product, build trust in what they see, and feel confident enough to put their money down. PDP vs PLP: what is the difference? Product detail pages and product listing pages look relatively similar but serve different roles in the customer journey. A product listing page (PLP) helps shoppers discover and compare multiple products through category pages, collections, or search results. A product detail page (PDP) is the next step in the funnel. It helps shoppers move from comparison to evaluation by providing the detailed information needed to make a purchase decision. While there is some overlap between the two, this guide focuses specifically on the product detail page: the moment where shopper interest turns into purchase intent. PLP PDP Purpose Browse multiple products Evaluate one product Shopper intent Discovery Purchase decision Content Product grids, filters, thumbnails Images, descriptions, reviews, variants Image role Capture attention Build trust and confidence Main KPI Click-through rate Conversion rate Information depth Summary-level Detailed Mobile behavior Fast scrolling Product evaluation AI focus Discoverability Structured product data and metadata Why the PDP has become the new storefront E‑commerce is heavily visual. Shoppers move through product grids the same way they scroll social feeds: quickly, instinctively, and with little patience for long blocks of text. In physical retail, shoppers can touch fabrics, inspect materials, and judge scale in person. Online stores rely on product images to recreate that experience. The strongest PDPs are designed to eliminate doubt. They help shoppers understand the product, assess its quality, and make a purchase decision with confidence. On mobile, which now drives roughly three-quarters of e‑commerce traffic and about 60% of online sales, visual content plays a critical role in that process. Shoppers notice inconsistency more than brands often realize. Photoroom’s State of GenAI in Marketplaces (2026) report found that 63% of shoppers said inconsistent product images lower trust in a marketplace or seller. Those expectations are no longer limited to enterprise retailers. Marketplaces and social commerce platforms have normalized high visual standards across e‑commerce UX. Regardless of whether someone is shopping from a global retailer or a small online store, the expectations are increasingly the same: Clear product photography Uniform image styling Accurate colors Visible texture and detail Realistic scale references Fast-loading mobile galleries High-quality product photography is the baseline shoppers expect. The competitive advantage comes from repeatable systems that maintain cohesive product photography across an entire catalog, regardless of how many products a business sells. The impact goes beyond aesthetics. Improvements in the visual quality of product images increasingly translate into measurable business outcomes. In Photoroom’s Hidden Cost of Product Photography for SMBs (2026) report, sellers who tracked the results of improving their product images reported a median uplift of 30% in sales or conversion rate. As shopper expectations continue to rise, product photography is becoming one of the most important drivers of product page performance. The brands that win are not necessarily those creating the most content, but those building the most effective visual systems. Defining the new standard for high-performing product pages Today’s strongest product pages combine clear and consistent product images , mobile-first design, structured information and scalable systems that help businesses convert more shoppers and grow more efficiently. Increasingly, they must also serve a second audience: AI systems. Product pages are no longer interpreted only by shoppers. AI-powered search experiences, recommendation engines, and shopping agents now rely on images, structured metadata, product schema, and catalog consistency to evaluate and recommend products. The brands that optimize for both human shoppers and AI systems already hold the competitive advantage. This shift is redefining what great product content looks like. Enterprise retailers are looking for ways to scale visual consistency across millions of products, while smaller businesses can now access capabilities that were once reserved for brands with dedicated studios and merchandising teams. For the first time, growing e‑commerce brands can compete with product experiences traditionally associated with the industry's largest retailers. Photoroom’s State of GenAI in Marketplaces (2026) report found that 87% of shoppers ranked product visuals as the most important factor influencing purchase decisions. As visual commerce becomes more competitive, images are no longer just a creative asset, it's a growth lever. Six essential jobs every product detail page must do After reviewing product pages across marketplaces, retailers, and direct-to-consumer brands, we've found that the strongest PDPs are remarkably similar beneath the surface. While categories, aesthetics, and brand positioning may vary, effective product pages excel across six core areas. Together, these six jobs provide a useful framework for evaluating product page quality. Weakness in any one area can create friction, reduce trust, or leave shopper questions unanswered. The strongest PDPs balance all six. Job Why it matters Product fidelity and trust Reduces uncertainty and return risk Image realism and craft Builds confidence through believable, authentic images Brand distinctiveness Strengthens recognition and memorability Visual consistency Reinforces confidence across products and categories Conversion focus Guides buyers toward confident purchase decisions Image type coverage Improves clarity by answering shopper questions more completely 1. Product fidelity and trust Product fidelity is the degree to which a product page accurately represents what a customer will receive. The strongest PDPs make products easy to evaluate online by showing accurate color, materials, texture, scale, and construction. Detail photography, close-ups, and image type coverage help bridge the gap between digital browsing and physical inspection. Fidelity when done well not only builds trust, it reduces returns. Photoroom's photography and photo-editing trends research revealed that 22% of product returns are driven by discrepancies between a product's online appearance and its real-world appearance. The more accurately a PDP represents color, texture, materials, and scale, the less likely shoppers are to feel disappointed after purchase. The stakes are large: the National Retail Federation estimated that U.S. retailers will see $849.9 billion in merchandise returns in 2025, including 19.3% of online sales. 2. Image realism and craft Strong product photography is not only about showing the product clearly. It is also about presenting it thoughtfully and believably. A product should appear naturally integrated into its environment, with convincing scale, lighting, perspective, and physics that the human eye accepts instinctively. Composition reinforces that realism through strong framing, thoughtful use of negative space, visual hierarchy, and controlled art direction. The strongest PDPs combine intentional composition with visual authenticity. Whether the style is minimal and functional or highly art directed, products should sit naturally within their surroundings, with accurate proportions and interactions with environmental elements that hold up both at a glance and under closer inspection. Even subtle inconsistencies, unnatural lighting, impossible shadows, distorted details, or other AI artifacts, can make an image feel “wrong”. When shoppers lose confidence in the image, conversion suffers as a result. 3. Brand distinctiveness Strong PDPs communicate a recognizable and unified point of view through composition, lighting, styling, color treatment, and art direction. This goes beyond making images look attractive; it establishes a distinct visual and sensory identity that expresses what the brand stands for. The goal is to build a visual signature that shoppers can recognize instantly, even before they see a logo. Brand distinctiveness is not simply the result of creative execution, but of a deliberate and consistent expression of a unique value proposition. It is how a brand chooses to present its products, through tone, styling, and curation, in a way that feels inherently specific to them. Over time, this disciplined expression becomes part of the brand itself. 4. Visual consistency Visual consistency is one of the clearest indicators of a well-executed product experience. Lighting, backgrounds, image angles, cropping, shadows, and styling should feel connected across the entire catalog, not just for the hero shots. The strongest brands will apply the same visual language across hero images, variants, lifestyle photography, and supporting assets. This consistency reduces cognitive load by making it easier for shoppers to compare products and navigate the catalog without reinterpreting each image. Professional, cohesive presentation also reinforces confidence in the brand and allows the product itself to remain the focus. Shoppers notice inconsistency more than brands often realize. When products appear to have been photographed using different standards, the experience can feel fragmented, leading shoppers to question the brand’s reliability. Consistency signals operational maturity, while inconsistency introduces unnecessary risk. 5. Conversion focus A product page is not simply an image collection. It is a decision-making environment where images carry the primary weight of evaluation. While image sequencing shapes the journey, it is the individual images themselves that drive perception and ultimately influence choice. The strongest galleries support this by presenting visuals in a deliberate order that moves shoppers from initial interest through to purchase confidence, answering key questions along the way. A typical sequence might move from hero images to alternate product angles, lifestyle context, detail shots and scale references. Every image should answer a question about fit, material, functionality, quality, or use case. When image sequencing is structured intentionally, the collection flow helps shoppers move from curiosity to confidence with less friction. 6. Image type coverage No single image can answer every shopper question. The strongest PDPs vary image types, with each one serving a different purpose in the shopping funnel. This might include: Lifestyle images to create desire and help shoppers imagine the product in real life, often serving as the first point of engagement in ads, social content, and other discovery channels Hero images to establish instant product recognition and drive clicks from search results, category pages, and product listing pages (PLPs) Product views and alternate angles to help shoppers evaluate the item and understand its overall appearance Detail and macro shots to showcase materials, craftsmanship, texture, and quality Scale and fit references to remove uncertainty and give shoppers the confidence to purchase Coverage should match the needs of the category. A beauty product may require texture shots and ingredient visuals, while furniture may require room placement images and scale references. Each image should contribute new information rather than repeating the same perspective. The anatomy of great product page design One of the most common mistakes brands make is treating product images as individual assets rather than part of a decision-making system. Effective product page optimization starts with understanding that images should work together to guide shoppers through the buying journey. The strongest PDPs use structured image galleries where each visual answers a different question, building purchase confidence. The gallery deserves this attention: images are the first element 56% of desktop shoppers explore on a product page, and 42% try to judge a product’s size from the images alone ( Baymard Institute ). Hero images Capture attention instantly Hero images are often the first product visuals shoppers encounter in search results, category pages, and marketplaces. Their job is to communicate the product clearly at a glance. In many cases, they determine whether a product sells at first sight. For food platforms , effective hero images focus attention on the meal itself, helping shoppers quickly assess ingredients, portion size, and overall appeal. Tools such as AI Retouch can help remove distractions so the product remains the focal point. Lifestyle images Create emotional and practical context Lifestyle images help shoppers imagine products in real situations. Whether showing clothing in motion, furniture inside homes, or beauty products during application, these visuals make products feel more relatable and believable. A studio product shot may show an armchair clearly, but a lifestyle image reveals how it fits into a real room. This practical context often plays a major role in the purchase decision. AI Product Staging makes it possible to create contextual scenes without the cost and complexity of traditional location photography. Detail and macro shots Show texture and quality Detail photography reveals texture, craftsmanship, finishes, and material quality that shoppers cannot inspect in person. Video and short-form motion can strengthen this further by showing how materials move and behave in use. For a luxury wool coat, close-ups of fabric texture, stitching, and finishing details help justify a premium price point. Video Generator can show how the garment moves, hangs, and drapes on the body, providing quality cues that help explain what separates a $2,000 coat from a $200 alternative. Variant images Support comparison Strong variant galleries help shoppers compare colors, finishes, and product options clearly. Lighting, framing, and image angles should stay uniform across every variation so differences feel easy to evaluate. We often see apparel brands photograph a black dress on a model while showing the red version as a flat lay. This means that shoppers end up comparing presentation styles rather than comparing colors. Tools such as Recolor help brands generate and manage product variants consistently, while applying edits in Batch Mode can streamline updates across large image sets. Scale references Reduce hesitation One of the biggest challenges in online shopping is judging size accurately. Simple visual clues such as model photography, hand-held shots, room placement, and dimension overlays help shoppers understand dimensions and proportions before purchasing. A necklace photographed on a white background may look elegant, but without any scale reference it's difficult to judge the length and where it sits when worn. Virtual Model helps brands create realistic scale references without organizing traditional photoshoots, reducing both production time and cost. In Photoroom’s survey of 1,356 e‑commerce sellers, 58% said they now create store-ready images in under five minutes instead of 15, saving more than 12 hours each month. Feature callouts Improve scannability Feature callouts turn important product details into visual explanations. Annotated images can often communicate dimensions, materials, or functionality faster than large paragraphs of text. For example, a skincare brand can highlight active ingredients and usage instructions directly within the images rather than relying solely on product copy. Add Text makes it easy to create clear visual annotations that surface important information at the moment shoppers are evaluating the product. Sequenced image galleries Guide product evaluation Product image sequencing is the order in which visuals appear on a product page. The most effective PDPs answer shopper questions progressively, moving from overall appearance to fit, materials, condition, and supporting details. Consider someone evaluating a vintage jacket online. They typically want to see the overall style and silhouette first, then assess the fit on a Ghost Mannequin from different angles, inspect the fabric texture and stitching, examine any signs of wear, and finally review labels, measurements, or other details that confirm authenticity. Product image sequencing works best when it mirrors this evaluation process, helping shoppers build confidence step by step rather than forcing them to search for information. Mobile product page design Optimize visuals for smaller screens Most PDP traffic now happens on mobile devices. Most product detail page (PDP) traffic now comes from mobile devices. According to Capital One , 59% of global e‑commerce sales are generated on mobile, and this share is projected to increase to 63% by 2028. As a result, mobile product page design should prioritize: Appropriate product sizing within the frame Consistent product positioning and alignment across images Visible product detail Optimized image file sizes Fast-loading galleries Clear swipe behavior Products should remain easy to evaluate on smaller screens without zooming excessively. A common issue we see with furniture retailers are visuals designed primarily for desktop. A beautifully styled living room may look impressive on a large monitor, but on a smartphone the sofa being sold can occupy only a small portion of the frame. Shoppers are left squinting to evaluate materials and construction. Tools such as Resize allow brands to adapt images for mobile-first browsing. Which e‑commerce brands are raising the standard Across categories, the best product pages follow similar principles even when their aesthetics differ. Rather than treating product images as standalone assets, they use visual content to answer shopper questions in a logical sequence, building purchase confidence. Fashion and beauty: demonstrating movement and texture Leading fashion brands use movement to communicate fit, drape, and fabric behavior. Static white-background photography still plays an important role, but shoppers increasingly expect richer visual experiences that help them understand how a garment will look and feel in real life. Mango and Zara have long set the standard in this area. Their product pages guide shoppers from inspiration to evaluation, moving seamlessly between aspirational imagery and more practical views of the garment. PDPs appear curated like luxury editorial; as customers scroll, they can see how fabrics hang on the body, how silhouettes change in motion, and how materials appear up close. A similar approach can be seen at Ann Mashburn . The brand uses carefully sequenced images that alternate between full-body views and detailed close-ups as the model moves naturally through the frame. The result is an almost cinematic browsing experience that helps shoppers evaluate fit, movement, texture, and craftsmanship progressively, with each image building on the last. Some retailers are also exploring new ways to scale these richer product experiences. Zalando, for example, has invested in digital twins, high-fidelity digital replicas of products and models that can be reused across merchandising content. The retailer's goal is to create more detailed and consistent product experiences while increasing content production efficiency. In March 2026, co-CEO David Schroeder said AI had enabled Zalando to produce "70% more content" at roughly the same cost ( Reuters , 2026). Beauty shoppers face a similar challenge: they need to evaluate products they cannot touch, smell, or apply before purchase. Rather than relying solely on pack shots, strong beauty PDPs use macro texture shots and demonstration content to show how products behave in real-world use. Erno Laszlo supplements traditional product photography with short video clips that show creams being applied to skin or serums dispensing from a bottle. Rather than simply showing the product, these assets help shoppers understand consistency, absorption, and finish before buying. Lake & Skye takes a complementary approach by incorporating ingredient information and product benefits directly within its images. The result is a PDP that functions as both a merchandising tool and an educational experience, helping shoppers understand not only what the product is, but why it may be right for them. Home: adopting effective contextual placement Home and furniture brands increasingly rely on contextual images to help shoppers visualize products in their own spaces. These purchases often depend on factors such as scale, proportion, materials, and how a product fits within an existing environment. The challenge is not simply showing the product, but helping shoppers imagine living with it. Live Outer provides a strong example of this approach, presenting outdoor furniture within carefully staged patios and backyard settings. Rather than isolating products against a plain background, the brand shows how pieces interact with their surroundings, helping shoppers understand scale, styling, and how the furniture might fit into their own outdoor spaces. Some brands extend this idea beyond physical placement and into ownership itself. Le Labo , for example, includes images of its signature labels being applied by hand, followed by the finished product carefully packaged for delivery. These visuals do more than communicate scale. They tell a story about craftsmanship, personalization, and the journey from purchase to unboxing, making it easier for shoppers to imagine the product arriving at, and becoming part of, their home. Common PDP mistakes hurting conversion Fixing these issues is often one of the fastest ways to improve product page conversion rate. Mistake What goes wrong Example Solution Every image says the same thing Repetitive galleries waste valuable PDP space without answering new shopper questions. A sweatshirt gallery may show front, back, and folded views, but never reveal fabric texture, fit on different body types, or styling context. The shopper sees the product repeatedly without learning anything new. Keep visual styling consistent , but ensure every image contributes new information. No scale reference Shoppers struggle to judge size or fit, increasing hesitation and return risk. A luxury candle is photographed beautifully on a white background and in a styled living room, but never beside a hand or familiar household object. Shoppers cannot tell whether the vessel is 6 ounces or 20 ounces. Add contextual images , room placement, model photography, or hand-held references. Inconsistent lighting, color grading and styling Products feel disconnected across the catalog, reducing trust. A furniture marketplace combines supplier-provided assets from hundreds of brands. One sofa appears in a professionally staged sunlit room, another on a white background, and a third in a dim smartphone photo, making the catalog feel fragmented and less trustworthy. Standardize lighting, shadows, crops, alignment and backgrounds across image sets. Unrealistic AI staging Distorted proportions, shadows, or textures damage credibility quickly. A food product appears illuminated from underneath, creating unnatural shadows that subconsciously make the scene feel artificial and less trustworthy because people instinctively expect light sources to come from above. Use realistic backgrounds , believable lighting, and manual corrections when needed. Low mobile readability Wide crops and small products become difficult to evaluate on phones. A bedding PDP opens with a wide master-bedroom scene where the duvet occupies less than a quarter of the frame. On a phone screen, shoppers can barely inspect the fabric, pattern, or stitching details. Use mobile-friendly image sizing, clear product framing , and optimized file formats to balance visibility and loading speed. Indistinguishable texture Shoppers struggle to judge material quality online. A premium cashmere blanket is shown only folded on a bed and draped over furniture. Without a close-up of the weave, fibers, or edge finishing, it looks nearly identical to a much cheaper synthetic alternative. Use close-up images and high-resolution exports to highlight texture clearly. Poor sequencing Disorganized galleries create friction instead of confidence. A handbag image collection begins with packaging, then a lifestyle image, then a zipper close-up, then a campaign photo before ever showing a straightforward front-facing view of the product. Structure galleries intentionally from hero images through to details and scale references . Overly artistic photography Stylized images can make products harder to evaluate. A skincare bottle is photographed through colored glass and dramatic shadows, making it difficult to see the packaging, label, or product size. Keep products recognizable with clean backgrounds , compositions and realistic lighting. Confusing variant presentation Inconsistent variant images increase uncertainty and return risk. One color of a sweatshirt is shown folded on a shelf, another on a model outdoors, and a third as a flat-lay studio shot. Shoppers struggle to determine whether differences are caused by the product or the photography. Maintain identical framing, lighting, and angles across all similar variants . Explore all Photoroom tools Future-proofing your PDPs for AI shopping agents A major shift is reshaping e‑commerce: products are more often being discovered, evaluated, and recommended by AI systems, not just human shoppers. An AI shopping agent is a system that helps consumers discover, compare, and choose products by interpreting information across search results to determine whether a product is trustworthy, relevant, and recommendation-worthy. What do AI shopping agents look for when evaluating a product page? AI shopping agents evaluate: Structured product schema (JSON-LD) Product titles and descriptions Alt text Image labels and filenames Variant consistency Price and availability Return policy information Catalog consistency Humans evaluate visuals instinctively. AI systems evaluate the underlying structure supporting those visuals. That means agent-ready PDPs need to work for both people and machines. Human shopper looks for AI shopping agent looks for Product images Structure product schema Visual trust signals Metadata consistency Lifestyle context Alt text and image labels Reviews and ratings Variant relationships Product benefits Structure attributes Emotional appeal Machine-readable organization Mobile usability JSON-LD markup Brand credibility Catalog consistency In practice, that means improving: Product page alt text Image alt text and labelling conventions Structured metadata Variant organization Product accuracy For example, a file named: product-image-4.jpg tells an AI agent very little. A filename like: black-leather-crossbody-bag-side-view.jpg provides much stronger product context. Managing these elements manually can quickly become difficult at scale, which is why many brands are investing in a well-structured product catalog. A centralized product catalog helps ensure that product data, image metadata, naming conventions, descriptions, and variant information remain consistent across channels while making products easier for AI agents and search engines to interpret. Many catalog management platforms now help automate these processes, including SEO-friendly file naming, alt text generation, product title and description creation, metadata enrichment, and variant organization. For example, tools such as Shopify catalog can help brands maintain accurate, structured product information across large inventories, improving both operational efficiency and product discoverability. What feeds AI search and shopping agent recommendations? Metadata alone is not enough. To improve visibility across AI-powered discovery channels, brands need structured product data that both AI search systems and shopping agents can easily interpret. Whether a consumer is asking ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI Overviews, or a dedicated shopping agent for product recommendations, these systems rely heavily on machine-readable information to understand products and determine which results to surface. Structured product schema, typically implemented through JSON-LD markup, helps provide that context. Key fields include: Product name Product images Pricing Availability Reviews and ratings Return policy information When this information is structured correctly, AI search systems can more accurately understand and reference products in generated responses, and AI shopping agents can evaluate products against user preferences, compare options, and make more confident recommendations. Brands that invest in structured product data are therefore better positioned to appear across a growing range of AI-powered discovery experiences. Brands that do not may become less visible even if the products themselves are strong. The future of visual commerce will be shaped by both human shoppers and AI systems. The brands that succeed will build product experiences that earn trust from both. As AI-assisted search and commerce continues to evolve, maintaining machine-readable product catalogs becomes a larger operational challenge, especially for marketplaces and retailers managing thousands of SKUs . That is why scalable visual systems matter more than ever. Building scalable product page systems across your catalog Great PDPs are where first impressions become purchase decisions. They succeed when every element, from images and product information to reviews, pricing, and delivery expectations, works together to drive conversions. The strongest PDPs use every image intentionally, from capturing attention to answering the questions shoppers need resolved before purchasing. Whether a brand manages 50 SKUs or 50,000, the goal remains the same: help shoppers move from curiosity to confidence. Every product page should answer key questions, reduce uncertainty, and make it easier to buy. What changes is the difficulty of maintaining that standard across a growing catalog. As e‑commerce becomes more visual, more mobile, and increasingly influenced by AI systems, the brands that stand out will be those that treat product images as a system rather than a collection of individual assets. They will build product pages that work for both human shoppers and the technologies helping them discover, evaluate, and compare products. As Anne-Claire Baschet at Mirakl , puts it: People buy pictures and receive products. – Anne-Claire Baschet, Chief Data & AI Officer, Agentic Commerce at Mirakl The best PDPs are built through clear standards, repeatable workflows, and a deep understanding of what shoppers need to see before they buy. summary: Scheduling friction costs health systems millions. Five9 Fusion for Epic turns EHR work queues into filled schedules - automatically.
body_text: Image What Your Patient Access Center's Scheduling Workflow Is Actually Costing You Healthcare Integrations & Partnerships AI & Automation Image Paresh Joshi Senior Product Management Director Paresh is a visionary product leader with 20+ years of experience building and scaling enterprise-grade technology products. He loves working closely with customers and cross-functional teams. He has built multiple products ground up driving million dollar revenue streams. At Five9 he owns a multi-product portfolio including industry vertical and platform product strategy driving Al-infused customer journeys. July 2, 2026 A patient needs to see a cardiologist. Her physician sent the referral two weeks ago. She’s called the patient access center three times. Each time, she’s waited more than four minutes on hold. Each time, she’s repeated the same information she gave on the call before. She still hasn't booked the appointment. This isn’t an edge case. It's the median patient scheduling experience at most health systems — and it plays out thousands of times a day at contact centers built to handle volume but never designed to eliminate friction. The numbers confirm what access leaders already feel A December 2025 MGMA Stat poll asked practice leaders their top patient access priority for 2026. The results were nearly tied: no-shows (27%), online scheduling (24%), phone access (22%), and wait times (21%). Years of technology investment have not resolved any of these. Additionally, the poll found that 71% of practices have fewer than one in four patients using digital tools to self-schedule and 42% of medical groups now charge no-show fees. Five use cases that define scheduling performance Where does scheduling actually break down, and what changes when the contact center and the EHR work from the same data? Here’s what that looks like in practice. 1. Inbound calls: eliminating friction at the moment that matters most When a contact center is natively integrated with the electronic health record (EHR) scheduling module, the patient’s profile surfaces before the call is answered. Authentication takes seconds. AI-powered guidance helps the agent select the right visit type, check availability against insurance and provider preferences, and book the appointment. Post-call, AI-generated documentation writes back to the EHR automatically, eliminating the three-to-five minutes of after-call work that follows every interaction today. 2. AI agents for routine volume: no hold time required Primary care follow-ups, annual wellness visits, post-operative checks, prescription management — most scheduling calls are predictable and don’t need a live agent. AI agents connected to real-time EHR data through open APIs handle these conversations across voice, SMS and digital channels, any hour of the day. According to SS&C Blue Prism's Global Enterprise AI Survey 2025 , 55% of healthcare organizations are fully implementing AI tools for patient scheduling and waitlist management. 3. Outbound campaigns from EHR work queues: turning passive failure into active engagement A typical health system’s EHR work queues hold referrals placed weeks ago that were never scheduled, patients overdue for follow-up and preventive outreach that never got started. None of these patients are calling. Their care gaps just keep widening. When the contact center connects directly to EHR work queue data, a referral aging past a defined threshold automatically triggers patient outreach — voice, SMS or portal notification — that either completes the booking through an AI agent or routes the patient to a live scheduler who already has full context loaded. It’s the same approach that helped Lumexa Imaging unlock $4 million in untapped revenue by automating outbound outreach and fixing call misrouting across millions of scheduling interactions. 4. Appointment reminders: reaching patients before they disappear A 2026 systematic review of 10 randomized controlled trials found that structured reminders improve outpatient attendance by 11% across SMS and telephone interventions. AI-driven live outreach targeted at high-risk patients produced statistically significant additional reductions, with the largest gains narrowing health equity disparities in appointment completion. A multi-touch sequence — confirmation at booking, a reminder one week out, an SMS three days before, then a live call for high-risk patients — consistently outperforms any single reminder. Every interaction updates the EHR in real time, and cancellations trigger automatic waitlist fills. 5. Referral-to-appointment conversion: closing the loop most health systems leave open A peer-reviewed analysis of 103,737 referral scheduling attempts found that only 34.8% resulted in a documented, completed specialist appointment. That’s nearly two thirds of referrals quietly disappearing, with no agent and no system ever flagging the gap. How Five9 Fusion for Epic addresses this directly Every use case above depends on one thing: the contact center and the EHR have to share a single source of truth. Without it, AI works with incomplete context, agents swivel between screens and outbound campaigns fire blind. Five9 Fusion for Epic is the CCaaS platform approved in Epic's Toolbox — Epic's own certification standard for native, API-driven integration. It connects Five9 directly to multiple Epic modules such as Epic Cadence (scheduling), Cheers (patient outreach) and Resolute (billing) with no middleware required. In scheduling terms, this means inbound calls arrive with the patient's full Epic record already on screen. AI Agents read real-time availability, book appointments and write confirmations back to Epic automatically. Outbound campaigns trigger from Epic work queues — aging referrals, care gaps, high-risk no-show predictions — and outcomes write back without a manual reconciliation step. Reminder sequences are calibrated against Epic's own no-show risk model, so high-risk patients receive a live outreach call, not just an automated text. The bottom line Scheduling is how a health system converts patient demand into delivered care, and clinical relationships into revenue. Every referral aging in a work queue, every no-show leaving a slot unfilled, every patient who couldn't get through — none of that is an operational inconvenience. It’s the cumulative cost of infrastructure built for volume and asked to deliver precision. Remember the cardiologist's patient from the opening? She's in an EHR work queue right now. Her referral is there. Her phone number is there. Her preferred contact channel is there. The only question left is whether your contact center is built to act on it. Ready to see it in action? title: How To Use the Jasper × Wrike Integration
summary: The Jasper Wrike integration sends content from Jasper straight into Wrike as a task—either a new one or one your team is already working on.
body_text: Marketing content rarely moves directly from creation to publication. A single campaign can pass through strategists, writers, designers, reviewers, regional teams, and outside agencies before it reaches the customer. Wrike gives teams a place to coordinate that work, from intake and assignments through approvals and delivery. But what it can’t do is produce content from a brand-governed source for each campaign, asset and variant. So the content gets made somewhere else, and then it has to travel. Someone downloads the draft, opens the right project, creates the task, attaches the file, and tags the reviewer. Do that once, and it is a minor chore. Do it across an intake queue, feeding four teams and a set of external partners, and the moving becomes the job. The bigger cost is not the clicks. It is what happens to the work in transit. Wrike's own Dark Matter of Work research found that up to 55% of the work inside an organization is invisible to the people who need to see it, in part because tools do not talk, which drives duplicated effort and wasted time. A draft attached to a task today is a snapshot. Edits keep happening in the source, the file on the task ages, and a reviewer three steps down the chain marks up a version already out of date. AI raises the stakes on that gap. When anyone can generate a campaign's worth of content in an afternoon, producing it is no longer the hard part. Scaling it responsibly is: keeping every piece on-brand, reviewed, and traceable as volume climbs. More output pushed through broken handoffs does not get you more done. It gets you more versions to reconcile, and more room for an off-brand or outdated piece to reach a customer. Responsible scale is achievable, but only when brand context and a single connected source travel with the work, instead of getting stripped away at each handoff. That is the difference between the appearance of scale and the real thing. What is the Jasper × Wrike integration? The integration connects on-brand content creation in Jasper Canvas and Grid to Wrike, where your team coordinates the work. Open a piece in Jasper, choose how it should travel, pick where it belongs, and export. Jasper creates a new task or adds to one already in the project, names it, and links back to the source. From there, the work is Wrike's to run: the assignee, the status, the approval path, its place in the wider work plan, and the reporting your team already relies on. Jasper produces the content. Wrike coordinates the people who touch it. A single blog post exports the same way as a full campaign. Generate a run of localized landing page sections and social variants in Grid in one sitting, and each piece lands in the right Wrike project as its own task, ready to route, instead of being carried over one file at a time. Why does it matter? Campaign work rarely stalls in the writing. It stalls in the handoffs, and in the doubt that creeps in when no one knows which file is current. A draft sits in a downloads folder for two days. A batch of variants lands in the wrong project. A reviewer pings the writer, asking where the latest version lives. By the time a piece clears the chain, someone has to stop and confirm it still matches what went out everywhere else. These delays are real, cumulative and costly. Because every piece is generated through Jasper IQ , the layer that holds your brand voice , approved messaging, and company knowledge , the content that lands in Wrike already reads like your brand. The version your team tracks and approves is one people can stand behind, and reviewers spend their time confirming accuracy, rather than rewriting voice from a raw draft. When the export carries a link back to the live Jasper doc, the task stays tied to its source, so the trail from creation to approval holds together instead of scattering across tools. That traceability is the point. In teams where work must survive an audit or compliance check, a task that links back to where the content came from is worth more than a file with no history. How do you set it up? Setup takes a couple of minutes and happens in two layers. A workspace admin enables Wrike once under Workspace Settings > Team Integrations, then each person connects their own Wrike account. No IT project and no waiting on a technical team. For step-by-step instructions, see the Jasper Help Center , or head straight to Workspace Settings in Jasper to connect. How do you send content from Jasper to Wrike? In Canvas or Grid, open the piece you want to send, select Export, and choose Wrike. Add the content to a task you are already working in, or create a new one, and it lands in the right project. Confirm Wrike is toggled on in the integrations panel the first time you use it. Choose how content travels with the task At export, you decide how the content reaches the team. Three options: Add a link to the Jasper doc. A link to the live document in Jasper is added to the Wrike task, so reviewers work in the source and every edit stays current. Best when you want one place, the latest version always lives. Attach the Jasper doc to the task. The content rides on the task as an attached Word file (.docx). Best when a stakeholder needs to open, mark up, or pass along the copy without a Jasper seat. Save to cloud storage, then link from the task. The document is saved to your connected cloud storage, such as SharePoint or Google Drive, and a link to it is added to the task. Best for teams that keep final assets in one library and want the task to point there. Routing every export to the same destination pulls scattered reviews back into one place and keeps the Wrike task tied to a single source, so the version of record does not fragment as it moves. How marketing teams put this to work If your team runs on Wrike and produces content at real volume, the integration fits a job you already do every week: turn an intake request into on-brand content and move it through the right hands-on time. Three ways that plays out. Marketing operations running an intake model An ops team fields requests from across the business through Wrike forms, then routes each one to the right owner. With the integration, the content generated against the brief in Jasper exports straight into the matching Wrike task, so the request and its deliverable stay together from intake to delivery instead of living in two systems. Creative and agency teams coordinating with outside partners A team working with external designers, freelancers, or an agency needs everyone touching the same current version. Export each finished piece into the shared Wrike project, attach the file or link the source, and partners pick it up where the rest of the work is tracked, without a Jasper seat and without a separate email thread carrying the latest draft. Regulated teams that need a traceable version of record A marketing team in healthcare or financial services has to show its work: which version went to review, when, and where it came from. Exporting from Jasper into Wrike with a link back to the source gives each task a clear line from content to approval, so the trail holds up when compliance or an audit asks for it, instead of being reconstructed from folders and inboxes after the fact. Looking ahead When content has to be downloaded, renamed, re-uploaded, and hand-routed into a work management tool, campaigns inherit delays that compound as teams scale, and the version of record gets harder to trust with every handoff. The Jasper Wrike integration keeps content moving through the process your team already runs. Marketers stay in Jasper to create on-brand content. Coordinators stay in Wrike to assign owners, manage reviews, and track delivery. As AI makes it possible to produce more content than ever, the advantage goes to teams that can keep that content moving, and keep it traceable, from creation to customer. Frequently asked questions Does the Jasper Wrike integration work with both Canvas and Grid? ‍ Yes. You can send content to Wrike from both Jasper Canvas and Jasper Grid, including high-volume Grid runs. Each exported piece lands as a task in the project you choose, either a new task or one already there. How does the content reach the Wrike task? ‍ Three ways to export: add a link to the Jasper doc on the task, attach the content as a Word file (.docx), or save it to connected cloud storage such as SharePoint or Google Drive, and add a link to the task. Cloud storage must be connected first. Who needs to set it up? ‍ Setup happens in two layers. A workspace admin enables Wrike under Workspace Settings > Team Integrations, then each person connects their own Wrike account. Does the export keep a link back to the original content in Jasper? Yes. Each export can link to the live Jasper document, so the Wrike task stays tied to its source, and the current version is always one click away. How does this integration keep content on-brand as it moves across tools and channels? Brand control cannot live in one tool when the work does not. Every piece you create in Jasper is generated through Jasper IQ, the layer that applies your brand voice, approved messaging, and company knowledge to each output. Content is on-brand before it leaves Jasper, whether it lands in Wrike, a cloud storage library, or anywhere else your team works. As you scale volume, that standard holds across every surface instead of drifting tool by tool, so reviewers confirm accuracy rather than reset voice. Ready to get started? Find more on connecting Jasper to Wrike in the Help Center. ‍
